# Cerebellum

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Basics of neurology > Cerebellum*

[Original Article Link](/library/Lp0wJS)

---

## Summary

The cerebellum is the part of the hindbrain that lies within the <u>posterior cranial fossa</u>, inferior to the occipital lobes and <u>dorsal</u> to the <u>brainstem</u>. It consists of three lobes (the <u>anterior</u>, <u>posterior</u>, and <u>flocculonodular lobe</u>). Functionally, it is divided into three zones. These are the <u>cerebrocerebellum</u> (the <u>lateral</u> zones), which receives sensory information from the <u>cerebral cortex</u> and is responsible for the planning of movements that are just about to occur (motor planning); the <u>spinocerebellum</u> (the <u>vermis</u> and intermediate zones), which receives proprioceptive information from the <u>dorsal columns</u> of the spinal cord and is responsible for the coordination of movements (motor execution); and the <u>vestibulocerebellum</u> (the <u>flocculonodular lobe</u>), which receives information from the <u>vestibular nuclei</u> and <u>visual cortex</u> and is responsible for balance and <u>ocular movements</u>. The <u>cerebellar cortex</u> transmits the information received from the three afferents (i.e., the <u>cerebrum</u>, spinal cord, and <u>vestibular nuclei</u>) to the four cerebellar <u>nuclei</u> (dentate, emboliform, globose, and fastigial) within the inner <u>white matter</u>. The cerebellar <u>nuclei</u> send efferent impulses to the <u>thalamus</u>, <u>red nucleus</u>, and <u>reticular formation</u> to execute cerebellar functions. The cerebellar tracts travel through the <u>cerebellar peduncles</u>.

---

## Gross anatomy

### Overview [[1]](/library/wkYhJ6)




* Location

* <u>Posterior cranial fossa</u> above the <u>foramen magnum</u>

* Inferior to the occipital and <u>temporal lobes</u>

* Covered by the <u>tentorium cerebelli</u> (<u>dura mater</u>)

* Connected to <u>brainstem</u> via three paired peduncles

* Separated from the medulla and <u>pons</u> by the <u>fourth ventricle</u>

* Function

* Control of balance and <u>ocular movements</u>

* Planning of movements that are about to occur

* Coordination of complex and sequential movements

* Maintenance of muscle tone

### Structure [[2]](/library/ES08Yf)[[3]](/library/9kYNJ6)




* The 2 hemispheres of cerebellum are separated in the midline by the cerebellar vermis.

* The cerebellar tonsil is an ovoid lobule located on the inferomedial aspect of each <u>cerebellar hemisphere</u>, above the <u>foramen magnum</u>

* Sulci and fissures further divide the cerebellum into lobes (see “Lobes and fissures” below)

> [!NOTE]
> <u>Cerebellar tonsil herniation</u> through the <u>foramen magnum</u> can occur due to a <u>Chiari malformation</u> or an increase in <u>intracranial pressure</u>, resulting in <u>brainstem</u> compression and cardiopulmonary arrest.




#### Lobes and fissures




* Three lobes

* <u>Anterior</u> lobe

* <u>Posterior</u> lobe

* <u>Flocculonodular lobe</u>

* Main fissures

* The primary fissure separates the <u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> lobes.

* The posterolateral fissure separates the <u>posterior</u> lobe from the <u>flocculonodular lobe</u>.

#### Cerebellar peduncles




* Three pairs of <u>cerebellar peduncles</u> connect the cerebellum to the <u>brain stem</u>.

* Afferent and <u>efferent cerebellar tracts</u> travel through the peduncles to and from the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>cerebellar cortex</u>.





| Peduncle | Characteristics | Tracts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Superior cerebellar peduncles (<u>SCP</u>) | <br><br>* Connects the cerebellum to the <u>midbrain</u><br><br>* Major <u>efferent pathway</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Efferent tracts from the deep <u>nuclei</u> of the cerebellum to the <u>contralateral</u> cortex<br><br> |
| <br>Middle cerebellar peduncles (<u>MCP</u>) | <br><br>* Connects the cerebellum to the <u>pons</u><br><br>* Largest peduncle<br><br>* Major <u>afferent pathway</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Afferent tracts from the <u>contralateral</u> cortex (pontocerebellar mossy fiber pathway)<br><br> |
| <br>Inferior cerebellar peduncles (<u>ICP</u>) | <br><br>* Connects the cerebellum to the medulla and spinal cord<br><br>* Afferent and <u>efferent pathways</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Afferent tracts carrying <u>ipsilateral</u> proprioceptive information from the spinal cord<br><br>* Efferent tract composed primarily of Purkinje cell <u>axons</u><br><br><br> |










> [!NOTE]
> Cerebellar lesions cause neurological deficits on the <u>ipsilateral</u> side!




### Vasculature of the cerebellum [[2]](/library/ES08Yf)




* <u>Arteries</u>

* <u>Basilar artery</u>

* <u>Superior cerebellar artery</u> (<u>SCA</u>) → superior surface of the cerebellum
* Also supplies the superior and <u>middle cerebellar peduncles</u> and the <u>midbrain</u>

* <u>Anterior inferior cerebellar artery</u> (<u>AICA</u>)→ <u>anterior</u> surface of the cerebellum
* Also supplies the <u>middle cerebellar peduncle</u> and inferolateral <u>pons</u>

* <u>Vertebral artery</u>
* Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)→ <u>posterior</u> surface of the cerebellum
* Also supplies the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncles</u> and the inferolateral medulla

* <u>Veins</u>: the <u>cerebellar veins</u> drain into the <u>transverse sinuses</u> and the <u>superior petrosal sinuses</u>.

## Functional zones of the cerebellum

| Zones of cerebellum |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Cerebrocerebellum | Spinocerebellum | Vestibulocerebellum |
| Corresponding cortex | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> hemispheres<br><br> | <br>* <u>Vermis</u> and intermediate zones<br><br> | <br>* <u>Flocculonodular lobe</u><br><br> |
| Corresponding <u>nuclei</u> | <br>* <u>Dentate nucleus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Emboliform nucleus</u><br><br>* <u>Globose nucleus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vestibular nuclei</u><br><br>* <u>Fastigial nucleus</u><br><br><br> |
| Input | <br><br>* <u>Cerebral cortex</u><br><br>* The <u>inferior olivary nucleus</u> of the medulla<br><br><br> | <br>* Spinal cord <br><br>* <u>Vermis</u>: input from the trunk and <u>proximal</u> portions of the limbs<br><br>* Intermediate zones: <u>distal</u> portion of the limbs<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vestibular nuclei</u> of <u>cranial</u> nerve VIII<br><br>* <u>Superior colliculi</u> and <u>visual cortex</u><br><br><br> |
| Function | <br><br>* Planning and execution of movements<br><br>* Coordination of complex and sequential motor movements<br><br>* Nonmotor functions: <u>cognition</u>, language, <u>learning</u>, and emotions<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Coordination of body and limb movement<br><br>* <u>Vermis</u>: central body (trunk, head, and <u>proximal</u> limbs)<br><br>* Intermediate zones: <u>distal</u> limbs (hands, fingers, feet, toes)<br><br>* Maintenance of muscular tone<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Balance<br><br>* <u>Ocular movements</u> and gaze stability<br><br><br> |
| Effect of lesions | <br><br>* Abnormal coordination of <u>ipsilateral</u> voluntary movements: <br><br>* Fall towards the side of the lesion (<u>ipsilateral</u>)<br><br>* <u>Dysdiadochokinesis</u><br><br>* <u>Dysmetria</u><br><br>* <u>Intention tremor</u><br><br>* Scanning speech (<u>ataxic dysarthria</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vermis</u>: trunk and <u>proximal</u> limb muscles affected<br><br>* <u>Truncal ataxia</u><br><br>* <u>Gait ataxia</u> (wide-based, unsteady gait)<br><br>* Tilting of the head<br><br>* Intermediate zones: <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>distal</u> limb muscles affected<br><br>* Limb <u>ataxia</u><br><br>* <u>Dysdiadochokinesis</u><br><br>* <u>Dysmetria</u><br><br>* <u>Intention tremor</u><br><br>* <u>Hypotonia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vertigo</u><br><br>* <u>Nystagmus</u><br><br><br> |





For further information on the effects of cerebellar lesions, see “Clinical features” in <u>cerebellar syndromes</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> A tip to remember the symptoms of cerebellar lesions: lesions of the <u>medial</u> part of cerebellum (i.e., <u>vermis</u>, <u>flocculonodular lobe</u>, and corresponding deep <u>nuclei</u>) affect <u>medial</u> structures (i.e., axial and <u>proximal</u> limb musculature), resulting in symptoms including <u>truncal ataxia</u> and <u>nystagmus</u>. Lesions of the <u>lateral</u> parts of cerebellum (i.e., the hemispheres) affect <u>lateral</u> structures (<u>distal</u> limb musculature), resulting in symptoms such as <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>limb ataxia</u>.

## Microscopic anatomy

The cerebellum is composed of the outer <u>gray matter</u> (<u>cerebellar cortex</u>) and inner <u>white matter</u> (cerebellar medulla).




### Cerebellar cortex [[5]](/library/aOYQI6)




* Receives afferent inputs from the <u>cerebrum</u>, spinal cord, and <u>vestibular nuclei</u>

* Sends neural impulses to the cerebellar <u>nuclei</u>

* Composed of 5 types of neuronal cells, densely packed and arranged in 3 layers

* The cortex is primarily an inhibitory structure; all cerebellar cells except <u>granule cells</u> are inhibitory.





| Layer | Cell types | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Molecular layer (outermost layer) | <br><br>* Basket cells: large <u>axons</u> with sparse <u>dendrites</u> (inhibitory)<br><br>* Cerebellar stellate cells: star-shaped <u>neurons</u> with multiple arborizations (inhibitory)<br><br>* Parallel fibers (<u>axons</u> of <u>granule cells</u>) and <u>dendrites</u> of Purkinje cells<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Receives excitatory input from <u>parallel fibers</u><br><br>* Sends inhibitory impulses to Purkinje cells<br><br><br> |
| <br>Purkinje cell layer (middle layer or ganglionic layer) | <br>* Cerebellar Purkinje cells (inhibitory)<br><br>* Flat <u>neurons</u> with fan-like dendritic projections<br><br>* <u>Axons</u> run perpendicular to the <u>parallel fibers</u> of the <u>granule cells</u><br><br>* The only output of <u>cerebellar cortex</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Receive excitatory input from <u>climbing fibers</u> and <u>granule cells</u><br><br>* Send inhibitory impulses to the deep cerebellar <u>nuclei</u> and thereby control the output of all motor coordination of the cerebellum<br><br><br> |
| <br>Granular layer of the cerebellum (inner layer) | <br><br>* Golgi cells: located in the upper portion of the granular layer<br><br>* Granule cells (excitatory): small, densely packed <u>neurons</u> that secrete <u>glutamate</u><br>* Most abundant cell type in the cerebellum<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Golgi cells</u>: receive excitatory impulses from the <u>molecular layer</u> and send inhibitory impulses to the <u>granule cells</u><br><br>* <u>Granule cells</u>: receive excitatory input from <u>mossy fibers</u> and send excitatory efferents to the Purkinje cells<br><br><br> |





![Normal cerebellar cortex](media/g51pfnuta1u67r3uiqrcyk8b.jpg)

Normal cerebellar cortex




### Cerebellar medulla




* Composed of <u>climbing fibers</u>, <u>mossy fibers</u>, Purkinje cell <u>axons</u>, and the deep cerebellar <u>nuclei</u>

* Mossy fibers : afferent <u>axons</u> from the <u>cerebral cortex</u>, <u>pons</u>, spinal cord, and <u>vestibular nuclei</u> to the cerebellum. Terminate on <u>granule cells</u> → send excitatory stimuli to the Purkinje cells.

* Climbing fibers: afferent <u>axons</u> from the <u>inferior olivary nuclei</u> of the medulla → terminate on Purkinje cells

* Four deep cerebellar <u>nuclei</u> (from <u>lateral</u> to <u>medial</u>): dentate, emboliform, globose, and <u>fastigial nucleus</u>

* For information on the function and neural pathways of the cerebellar medulla, see “Cerebellar tracts” below.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Glutamate</u> is the <u>neurotransmitter</u> of <u>granule cells</u>, which are the only excitatory cerebellar cells. <u>GABA</u> is the inhibitory <u>neurotransmitter</u> of all other cerebellar cells.




> [!NOTE]
> Purkinje cells provide the only efferent effect from the <u>cerebellar cortex</u> to the cerebellar <u>nuclei</u>, and, thus, play an essential role in the regulation of cerebellar output!




> [!NOTE]
> Purkinje cells are inhibitory!

## Cerebellar tracts

### <u>Afferent cerebellar tracts</u> (input) [[4]](/library/Tea6yj)[[10]](/library/o0Y0Sn)




* Afferent tracts arise from three main sources: the <u>cerebral cortex</u>, the spinal cord, and the vestibular nerve.

* Afferent tracts are excitatory and travel to the cerebellum via <u>mossy fibers</u> and <u>climbing fibers</u>.

* Afferent tracts travel mainly through the inferior and <u>middle cerebellar peduncles</u>.





| Afferent cerebellar tracts |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Source | Tracts | Course | Function |
| <u>Cerebral cortex</u> | <br>* Corticopontocerebellar tract<br><br> | <br>* <u>Cerebral cortex</u> → corona radiata → <u>internal capsule</u> → <u>pontine nuclei</u> → <u>mossy fibers</u> → <u>cerebellar hemisphere</u> via <u>middle cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br> | <br>* Motor planning, motor <u>learning</u>, and <u>cognition</u><br><br> |
| <br>* Cortico-olivocerebellar tract<br><br> | <br>* <u>Cerebral cortex</u> → corona radiata → <u>internal capsule</u> → <u>inferior olivary nuclei</u> → <u>climbing fibers</u> → <u>cerebellar hemisphere</u> via <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Corticoreticulocerebellar tract<br><br> | <br>* <u>Cerebral cortex</u> → corona radiata → <u>reticular formation</u> in <u>pons</u> and medulla → <u>mossy fibers</u> → <u>cerebellar hemisphere</u> via the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u> and <u>middle cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br> |  |  |
| Spinal cord | <br><br>* Spinocerebellar tract<br><br>* Dorsal spinocerebellar tract<br><br>* Ventral spinocerebellar tract<br><br>* Cuneocerebellar tract<br><br>* Rostral spinocerebellar tract<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Golgi tendon organs</u> and <u>muscle spindles</u> → <u>posterior horn</u> of the spinal cord → <u>mossy fibers</u> → <u>cerebellar hemisphere</u> via the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u> and <u>superior cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ipsilateral</u> proprioceptive information<br><br> |
| Vestibular nerve | <br>* Vestibulocerebellar tract<br><br> | <br>* Vestibular nerve → <u>vestibular nuclei</u> → <u>mossy fibers</u> → <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>flocculonodular lobe</u> via the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Proprioception</u><br><br> |










> [!NOTE]
> Excitatory input to the <u>cerebellar cortex</u> travels through <u>mossy fibers</u> and <u>climbing fibers</u>!




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Mossy fibers</u> terminate on <u>granule cells</u>. <u>Climbing fibers</u> terminate on Purkinje cells.




### Efferent cerebellar tracts [[10]](/library/o0Y0Sn)




* Efferent tracts originate from the four deep cerebellar <u>nuclei</u> and travel mainly via the <u>superior cerebellar peduncle</u>.

* The tracts of the <u>fastigial nucleus</u> travel via the <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u>.





| Tract | <u>Nucleus</u> | Course | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rubrospinal tract | <br>* Dentate nucleus<br><br> | <br>* <u>Dentate nucleus</u> → <u>superior cerebellar peduncle</u> → <u>thalamic nuclei</u> → <u>internal capsule</u> → corona radiata → <u>primary motor cortex</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Contralateral</u> motor coordination<br><br> |
| <br><br>* Emboliform nucleus<br><br>* Globose nucleus<br><br><br> | <br>* Globose and <u>emboliform nuclei</u> → <u>superior cerebellar peduncle</u> → <u>red nucleus</u> → <u>rubrospinal tract</u><br><br> | <br>* Tone of <u>contralateral</u> <u>skeletal muscles</u><br><br> |  |
| Cerebellovestibular tract | <br>* Fastigial nucleus<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Fastigial nucleus</u> → <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u> → bilateral <u>vestibular nuclei</u> → <u>vestibulospinal tract</u><br><br>* <u>Fastigial nucleus</u> → <u>inferior cerebellar peduncle</u> → bilateral <u>reticular formation</u> → <u>reticulospinal tract</u> → motor <u>neurons</u> from spinal cord<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Coordination of balance and <u>saccadic</u> <u>ocular movements</u><br><br>* Stretch reflex and motor movements<br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Deep cerebellar <u>nuclei</u> (from <u>lateral</u> to <u>medial</u>): "Don't Eat Greasy Food" (Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial).




> [!NOTE]
> The deep <u>nuclei</u> are the only output from the cerebellum.

## Embryology

The cerebellum derives from the hindbrain (<u>rhombencephalon</u>) and <u>metencephalon</u>.




For more information on the <u>embryology</u> of the nervous system, see “<u>Embryology</u>” in “<u>The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system</u>.”

## Clinical significance

* <u>Cerebellar defects</u>

* <u>Ataxia</u>

* <u>Dysmetria</u>

* <u>Dysarthria</u>

* <u>Scanning speech</u>

* <u>Dysdiadochokinesis</u>

* <u>Tremor</u>

* <u>Nystagmus</u>

* <u>Hypotonia</u>

* Hereditary <u>ataxias</u>

* <u>Friedreich ataxia</u>

* <u>Spinocerebellar ataxia</u>

* <u>Ataxia-telangiectasia</u>

* Acquired <u>ataxias</u>

* <u>Multiple sclerosis</u>

* <u>Cerebellar stroke</u>

* <u>Vitamin B12 deficiency</u>

* <u>Wilson disease</u> (accumulation of <u>copper</u> in the cerebellum)

* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u>

* Congenital cerebellar <u>malformations</u>

* <u>Chiari I malformation</u>

* <u>Chiari II malformation</u>

* <u>Dandy-Walker malformation</u>

* Cerebellar tumors

* <u>Cerebellar medulloblastoma</u>

* <u>Pilocytic astrocytoma</u>

* Cerebellar <u>metastases</u>

* <u>Hemangioblastoma</u>

* Other 

* <u>Foramen magnum herniation</u>

* <u>Neurological exam</u> (e.g., <u>finger-to-nose test</u>, <u>Romberg test</u>, <u>rapid alternating movement tests</u>, <u>heel-to-shin test</u>)
